narrative:
The model determined that you have an 88.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons for the negative outcome. Being in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. These academic standings are far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 also worked against you, though its influence was smaller; it is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average among those who were admitted.

Taken together, these performance indicators told the model that you would likely struggle to pass the bar exam, outweighing other details such as your middle family income, LSAT score of 29, full-time study plans, gender, and race (which were not used in the prediction).

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. These steps can demonstrate growth and better prepare you for the exam.
